newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole hurl accusations during debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole hurl accusations during debate.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican candidate Bob Dole on Sunday hurled accusations on the state of the economy, taxes, Medicare and foreign policy in their first face-to-face debate of campaign 1996.

"We are better off than we were four years ago. Let's keep it going," Clinton insisted, saying 10.5 million new jobs had been created during his tenure, that paychecks are rising, crime and welfare rolls are falling and America is at peace.

Dole, looking for an opening to derail Clinton's large lead in public opinion polls with Election Day a month away, quickly disagreed with the first in a series of sharp attacks he used throughout the night.

"Well, he's better off than he was four years ago," Dole said of Clinton, standing behind a podium a few feet away. Dole said some Americans may be better off but that generally "the American people are working harder and paying more taxes."
Dole said the centrepiece of Clinton's 1993 economic plan that the president says restored the U.S. economy included a tax increase that raised taxes on all Americans, not just the wealthy.
Clinton said Dole acknowledged earlier this year that the American economy is in its best shape in 30 years, but Dole said he doubted having said that.
On Medicare, the medical insurance for the elderly, Clinton charged the Republican balanced budget plan backed by Dole last year would make drastic cuts of $270 billion.
Clinton said Dole's opposition to Medicare goes back to 1965 when he voted against the creation of the programme.
Dole said he voted against it because he preferred an existing programme at the time and rebuked Clinton for using the issue to scare older Americans into voting for him.
"Stop scaring the seniors, Mr. President," Dole said. "You've already spent $45 million scaring seniors and tearing me apart. I think it's time to have a truce."

The face-to-face meeting was the first of two presidential debates between Democratic Clinton and Dole. A vice presidential debate between Democratic incumbent Al Gore and Dole's running mate Jack Kemp is scheduled for Wednesday.

Missing from the lineup was third-party candidate Ross Perot, judged by a commission to have no real chance of winning the election and thus excluded. He planned a television media blitz to try to recoup.
Dole was attempting to reverse an aura of inevitability that Clinton will be re-elected. Clinton's goal was to keep from making any major errors and do nothing to damage his large lead.

Dole, appearing nervous in the beginning, used his opening statement to point out some friends in the crowd, including Frank Carafa, who helped save him from death when he was injured in the Second World War.
The two candidates covered a great deal of ground, going after each other on issues such as drug use, the influence of special interest on campaigns and foreign policy.
Clinton extolled his handling of foreign policy, but Dole said the president has spent billions of dollars sending U.S. troops around the world.

Dole aggressively challenged Clinton's handling of foreign affairs. "He's deployed more troops than any president in history around the world," Dole said, complaining of U.S. commitments to U.N. peacekeeping efforts.
